Sarah: So for our project on the economics of festivals, do we still agree on comparing the Spring Festival travel rush with Western Christmas markets?
Tom: Yes, but we need to narrow it down. Comparing everything will be vague. Let's focus on one thing: holiday consumer behaviour — what people buy, why, and what that does to local economies.
Sarah: Agreed. My grandmother's town in Fujian comes alive every Lunar New Year — the temple fair, the sugar-painting stalls, the paper-burning rituals. Meanwhile last year in Basel, I saw Christmas market stalls selling gingerbread to tourists at triple the price locals would pay. Same festival logic, different mechanism.
Tom: I like that pairing — temple fairs versus Christmas markets. It shows both the cultural pull and the commercial layer on top.
Sarah: Shall we do interviews?
Tom: We have a sample problem. We only have time for about fifteen interviews. Fieldwork there is expensive — I'd need at least three days travelling.
Sarah: Alternatively, we collect secondary data — the National Bureau of Statistics publishes festive retail sales every year, and the EU does the same for December trade. Then interviews are only illustrative, not our evidence base.
Tom: That's more realistic. Two days of data cleaning versus a week of fieldwork — and the numbers will be stronger anyway.
Sarah: For the presentation, we need a structure. I'll do the introduction and the Chinese data section, you handle the European data and the comparative analysis, then we both discuss what each model gets right.
Tom: And our discussion chapter needs a critical angle — festive consumption isn't just tradition; it's engineered urgency. Marketing manufactures 'must-buy' lists for gifts, feasts and travel. Without them, what would we even celebrate?
Sarah: Careful — that sounds a bit cynical for academic writing.
Tom: But it's true and it's interesting. We can phrase it properly: 'commercialisation amplifies festive behaviour without replacing its cultural core' — that's an arguable thesis, not a rant.
Sarah: I like it. Now practicalities: our tutor said the report is due the 15th of January, four weeks before the symposium on the 12th of February.
Tom: Presentation first, then the written version?
Sarah: No — tutor said report first on the 15th, symposium in February. And we present slides, not a paper, at the symposium.
Tom: Right. And please, nobody start the data section with the 2019 baseline — use 2020 onward, that's the pre- and post-pandemic shift everyone cares about.
Sarah: Action items: I'll request the NBS data tomorrow, you grab the Eurostat reports by Friday, and we meet again on Wednesday to agree the interview questions.
Tom: Deal. One last thing — the bibliography. I hate doing bibliographies.
Sarah: Fine, I'll draft it early so we don't suffer later.
